newsitem.title: UK: Hong Kong seen at key juncture as market centre.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong seen at key juncture as market centre.

text.p: Just nine weeks ahead of the handover to China, Hong Kong stands of chance of becoming the third global financial centre behind London and New York, industry figures said on Wednesday. But many investors are wary and one prominent fund manager, emerging markets guru Mark Mobius, still sees the risk of it becoming a large but marginalised market. Edgar Cheng, chairman of the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong, sketched a scenario whereby Hong Kong will eclipse Tokyo as leading international financial centre in the Asian time zone while moving towards a day when it plays a central role in raising capital for a fast-growing Chinese hinterland.
"I see Hong Kong becoming the London of Asia and the Manhattan of China but it will take time." he said at a conference.
"I expect Shanghai to be predominately a domestic market, while Hong Kong will be the main international financial centre and the main link between China and the global market," Cheng said.

Mobius, president of Templeton Emerging Markets and co-ordinating manager of funds totalling $12 billion, has a different view. "Hong Kong stands a danger of becoming a Cantonese regional market," Mobius told Reuters at the conference.
He said Hong Kong's markets will grow along with the expanding pie in China but that "in five years or less Shanghai will be as important or more important than Hong Kong".
To increase Hong Kong's importance, Mobius called for the establishment of an Asian rival to Cedel and Euroclear that can serve as a central depository for bond and equity operations in the region.

"There should be an Asiaclear operation in the Asia timezone and I believe Hong Kong would be the perfect place to have such an operation. This is something that could go a long way towards establishing Hong Kong as a very important centre," Mobius said.

Mobius, whose Templeton Emerging Markets Group recently bought a floor of the Shanghai Stock Exchange building for $3 million in preparation for the handover, thinks that Hong Kong can help defend its position by fomenting liquidity in Asia region shares. He called for Hong Kong to have more international and regional issues listed on its exchange, a move he said would increase liquidity and open the door to more institutional investment.

Both Mobius and Cheng concur on the enormous potential of the region's capital markets, with China requiring trillions of dollars in infrastructure investment in coming years and Chinese investors eager to seek homes for the pools of cash amassed through their high savings rates.

Cheng is anticipating big changes over the next 10 years in the number of major Chinese companies or "red chips" that will list in Hong Kong. He said over the past three years 26 Chinese companies had listed in Hong Kong, raising about $4.5 billion but representing less than one percent of the bourse's market capitalisation.

"Following the reversion of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty, I believe these trends will gather further momentum," Cheng said, adding he sees potential for Hong Kong as a centre for derivatives based on Chinese shares or indices.

Cheng also sees potential for Hong Kong as the walls between mainland China and the rest of the world erode. "Hong Kong will play a leading part in this process, being first through each door as it opens.'

Mobius said his faith in Hong Kong as a financial centre has not diminshed but the handover to China carries risk. "There is a 70 percent chance of things going very, very well and a 30 percent chance of some accident happening and confidence in Hong Kong crashes.'
